tabs.title: Investigating the Problem
tabs.description: Interpret how the students found the source.

tabs.title: Using Evidence
tabs.description: Explain what the counts and interviews show.

questions.q: Why does the engineer encourage the students to look beyond the stream itself?
choices: The stream does not contain any real litter.
The students have no permission to make signs.
All the rubbish comes from the library.
The rubbish may have entered the water from drains elsewhere.
questions.explanation: The engineer traces a possible route from the street through a drain into the stream.

questions.q: What makes the students' first observations useful rather than just personal opinions?
choices: They ask only their closest friends.
They record counts in different street sections at a chosen time.
They take pictures of the stream once.
They choose the answer before investigating.
questions.explanation: The third paragraph describes a planned comparison with counts in five sections.

questions.q: What might explain the large difference between the bus stop and library counts?
choices: The library has no pavement.
The stream flows only past the bus stop.
The crowded stop and nearby full bin create more litter there.
The students counted for different months.
questions.explanation: The text connects high litter counts with the busy stop and overflowing bin.

questions.q: How did talking to a bus driver improve the investigation?
choices: It revealed that the bin was usually full by late afternoon.
It proved that students never dropped wrappers.
It showed that the stream contained no rubbish.
It changed the students' number of street sections.
questions.explanation: The bus driver provided a time-related explanation missing from the counts alone.

questions.q: Why is changing the bin's collection time a more focused solution than a warning sign?
choices: It makes customers stop buying snacks.
It removes every drain from town.
It prevents wind on other streets.
It addresses when the rubbish starts to build up.
questions.explanation: The council's change responds to the bin becoming full before the busy afternoon.

questions.q: Why do the students avoid claiming the problem has disappeared?
choices: They have not yet spoken to the café owner.
Wind and future storms could reveal other sources of litter.
They no longer need to observe the street.
The bus stop was closed for a month.
questions.explanation: The fifth paragraph explicitly leaves room for new weak points and changing weather.

questions.q: What is a strength of inviting neighbours to add photos to the map?
choices: It increases the amount of evidence beyond the original area.
It proves the café owner is responsible for everything.
It allows the students to delete unusual observations.
It makes rainwater flow in a different direction.
questions.explanation: More residents can contribute observations from streets the students did not survey.

questions.q: What does the final question shift attention towards?
choices: Designing a larger sign next to the stream.
Choosing a new name for the school project.
Finding where the litter enters the system in the first place.
Counting only rubbish in the water.
questions.explanation: The concluding question asks where the rubbish begins its journey.

questions.q: A school wants to protect a local stream. What should it investigate first?
choices: How many people enjoy taking photos by the water.
Where rainwater travels and where litter can enter drains.
Whether the river has a more attractive name.
Which students prefer the biggest classroom.
questions.explanation: The engineer shows how pavement litter can reach a stream through drains.

questions.q: What general lesson does the students' project suggest about environmental action?
choices: Simple signs always solve problems without further work.
People should clean only the part of the stream they can see.
Measurements are less useful than blaming one group.
Look for causes and adjust practical systems instead of blaming people immediately.
questions.explanation: The students use counts, interviews and a map before proposing practical changes.
